takeaways.text: The Stanford pipeline produces its first world-historical figure. Hoover proves the model — technical training plus capital access plus institutional network equals global leverage. The Second World War industrialises the insight.
California has learned to think at the scale of empire. The machinery is about to produce its first self-sustaining industry.

Railroad → land → Hoover (spine tie). Hoover's first employer was a land-speculation company that existed because "it was only when the transcontinental rail link was formed that full-blown settlement occurred and land prices boomed, creating the opportunity on which Minthorn and his partners intended to capitalize" (p. 26). The firm also owned the Salem Street Railway (p. 28). Its investors "drew few distinctions between the public's interest and their own" (p. 27). Hoover was among the first Americans to ride the newly opened rail route to Oregon (pp. 19–20).

Yale thread: Louis Janin — "educated at Yale and Freiburg," Comstock Lode and Rothschilds (p. 46). Janin's recommendation sent Hoover to Bewick, Moreing (p. 49). Lunch "likely at the Pacific Union Club on Nob Hill" (p. 47), Whyte's inference.

Public story vs. documented conduct (Janin hire). Hoover's memoir tells a charming copyist-to-engineer story. Whyte says the real hire rested on Hoover's usefulness to the North Star defense: he published a supposedly objective article in *Mining & Scientific Press* that matched North Star's case, without disclosing his tie to Janin, and was paid right after the verdict (pp. 47–48).

Panic of 1893 as hinge. It wiped out Minthorn's Oregon Land Co. and cost Hoover his USGS job (p. 45), the same downturn that hits Stanford's estate after Leland's death (cross-check with White, *Who Killed Jane Stanford?*). Whyte's frame: Hoover was "conceived in one economic depression" and "graduated into another" (p. 45).

Grant's Quaker Policy / Indian agents in the family. Guardian Lawrie Tatum was "one of President Grant's first Indian Agents," author of *Our Red Brothers* (p. 25 n.*³). Uncle Laban Miles was Osage agent (p. 16). A possible tie to Cardinal's land-dispossession thread. Moderate.

Branner patronage line. Hoover was office assistant from his second semester (p. 36). Branner arranged the Ozarks and Lindgren summers (pp. 37, 39–40) and advised him to turn down USGS for commercial mining (p. 48). Branner's own Edison and Boston-gold-mining past (p. 48).
